title: Concrete models with indexed Sets, Params, Vars and Constraints

blocks.text: 5.1.1 Concrete Models With Indexed Sets, Params, Vars and Constraints

GridCap's analytics team has inherited a set of planning scripts written in **Pyomo**, and its planners want the five-year model of lesson 6.4.1 (GridCap small: 40 projects, a budget for each of 2027 to 2031, a start window per project) available in the same tool, so the two teams can share one model. The model already exists in MathOpt, and lesson 6.4.1 printed its answer: NPV $24,260k, 27 of 40 projects started. This lesson ports it to Pyomo, one component at a time, and checks that the port gives the same plan. GridCap's data is fictional, as everywhere in this course.

The model comes from lesson 6.4.1, in section 6, which this course reaches later. You do not need to have read it: *The Model* below restates it in full. When this lesson says the port gives "the same numbers as lesson 6.4.1", it compares with the output that lesson recorded from its MathOpt model, solved with HiGHS on GridCap small, shown here as that lesson printed it:
<!-- unverified -->

OPTIMAL NPV $24,260k
started 27 of 40; 9 later than their earliest year
  P008 window 2029-2031 starts 2031  NPV 264 -> 182
  P010 window 2030-2031 starts 2031  NPV 26 -> 19
  P011 window 2029-2031 starts 2031  NPV 240 -> 140
  P012 window 2030-2031 starts 2031  NPV 201 -> 168
  P021 window 2028-2030 starts 2029  NPV 1,241 -> 1,012
  P025 window 2027-2029 starts 2028  NPV 1,009 -> 880
  P029 window 2030-2031 starts 2031  NPV 302 -> 233
  P031 window 2027-2028 starts 2028  NPV 1,000 -> 809
  P039 window 2027-2029 starts 2028  NPV 546 -> 386
starts per year: {2027: 4, 2028: 7, 2029: 4, 2030: 5, 2031: 7}

A line such as `P008 window 2029-2031 starts 2031  NPV 264 -> 182` is a deferred project: P008 may start in 2029, 2030 or 2031, the plan starts it in 2031, and its NPV falls from 264 (started in 2029) to 182. The module's tests rebuild lesson 6.4.1's MathOpt model and compare with it directly, so the comparison does not rest on this copy.

Pyomo is an **algebraic modeling language** written in Python: you declare named, indexed components (sets, data, variables, rows, an objective) much as they appear on paper, and Pyomo turns them into a matrix for whichever solver you choose. MathOpt (section 4) builds the same matrix from Python objects too, so the difference is in style, not in power. Pyomo's style is the one most textbooks and much inherited code use, which is why an interview may hand you Pyomo code.
The Model
The model being ported, as lesson 6.4.1 states it, with each label next to the name the Pyomo component gets.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`S = \{(i, t) : i \in P,\ t \in T_i\}`$ the allowed (project, start year) pairs, where $`T_i`$ is project $`i`$'s window; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups, each a set of projects; $`C`$ the pairs $`(c, t)`$ of a child project $`c`$ (parent $`p(c)`$, lag $`L_c`$ years) and one of its start years.

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ for $`(i, t) \in S`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ started in year $`t`$ ($k); $`\text{cost}_{i,t,y}`$, what project $`i`$ started in $`t`$ spends in calendar year $`y`$ ($k, 0 for a year it does no work); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`(i, t) \in S`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$. No variable exists outside $`S`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{(i,t) \in S} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**
A ConcreteModel Is Built From Data You Already Have

Pyomo has two kinds of model. A `ConcreteModel` is built immediately: every component you attach to it is constructed on the spot, from Python data you already hold. An `AbstractModel` declares the components first and receives the data later, from a data file or a dictionary passed to `create_instance()`. Everything in this course has its data in Python objects before the model is built (a GridCap `Portfolio`), so every model here is concrete; you will meet `AbstractModel` in older code and in the Pyomo book, and reading it only needs the extra step of where its data comes from.

A component becomes part of the model by being **assigned as an attribute**: `m.x = pyo.Var(...)` names the component `x` and registers it with `m`. The attribute name is the name the solver and every printout use.

import pyomo.environ as pyo

from gridcap import generate
from pyomo_timing import build

tiny = generate("tiny")

m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
`pyomo.environ` is the import that brings in the modeling components and the solver plug-ins; the course always imports it as `pyo`, as the Pyomo documentation does.
Sets Name the Indices, and a Set of Pairs Keeps a Sparse Index Sparse
A `Set` is a named collection of index values. `initialize=` takes any iterable, and Pyomo keeps the members in the order given (sets are ordered by default):

m.P = pyo.Set(initialize=[p.project_id for p in tiny.projects])
m.Y = pyo.Set(initialize=tiny.years)
m.S = pyo.Set(dimen=2, initialize=[(p.project_id, t) for p in tiny.projects for t in p.starts()])
print("P:", list(m.P))
print(f"P x Y has {len(m.P * m.Y)} pairs; S has {len(m.S)}:", list(m.S)[:4], "...")

`m.P * m.Y` is the **cross product**, every (project, year) pair: 8 × 3 = 24. A variable indexed by it would include starts outside every window, which lesson 6.4.1 avoided by never creating them. In Pyomo the same idea is a set whose members are the allowed pairs only: `m.S` holds 13, the same 13 start variables lesson 6.4.1 counted on tiny. `dimen=2` tells Pyomo each member is a pair, which it also checks when a member is added; it is required when Pyomo cannot see the size of the tuples, for example when the set starts empty. Such a set of tuples is called **sparse**: it lists the index combinations that exist instead of all the combinations the separate sets allow.

`m.M = pyo.Set(within=m.P, ...)` in `pyomo_timing.py` uses `within=` to declare the must-do projects a subset of the projects; Pyomo refuses a member outside it. A set can also be **indexed**: `m.members = pyo.Set(m.G, ...)` is one set of projects per alternative group, read as `m.members[g]`.
Params Hold the Data, and a Mutable Param Can Change After the Build

A `Param` is data keyed by a set. `initialize=` takes a dict from index to value. For an index inside the set but missing from the dict, `default=` supplies the value; for an index outside the set, Pyomo raises an error rather than invent a number:

npv[P001,2029] = 1077   budget[2027] = 2300
cost[P003,2027,2028] = 1490   cost[P003,2027,2029] = 0
npv[P001,2027]: KeyError "Index '('P001', 2027)' is not valid for indexed component 'npv'"

`m.cost` is indexed by `m.S, m.Y`: two sets as arguments make a three-part index (project, start year, calendar year). P003 started in 2027 spends 1,490 in 2028, its second year, and nothing in 2029, which comes from `default=0`, not from the dict. `npv["P001", 2027]` is refused because (P001, 2027) is not a member of `m.S`: P001 cannot start in 2027, so no NPV exists for it.

The budget is declared `mutable=True`. An ordinary (immutable) Param is replaced by its number when a row uses it, so the row holds 2300, and changing the data afterwards changes nothing. A mutable Param stays in the row as a name, and assigning a new value reaches every row that uses it:

full = build(tiny)
print("spend_cap[2027] upper side:", full.spend_cap[2027].upper, "=", pyo.value(full.spend_cap[2027].upper))
full.budget[2027] = 1500
print("after full.budget[2027] = 1500:", full.spend_cap[2027].upper, "=", pyo.value(full.spend_cap[2027].upper))

spend_cap[2027] upper side: budget[2027] = 2300
after full.budget[2027] = 1500: budget[2027] = 1500

The row's right side prints as `budget[2027]`, the Param itself, and `pyo.value` evaluates it to the current number. That is how a scenario study ("cut 2027 by $800k") re-solves the same model without rebuilding it. The price, according to the Pyomo documentation, is some extra work when the model is written out for the solver, so declare mutable only the data you will change.
A Var Takes Its Domain and Bounds From Its Declaration

A `Var` indexed by a set creates one variable per member. `domain=` is the set of values it may take: `pyo.Binary`, `pyo.NonNegativeReals`, `pyo.Reals`, `pyo.NonNegativeIntegers`, `pyo.Integers`, and `pyo.UnitInterval` for $`[0, 1]`$, among others. `bounds=` adds a lower and an upper bound, either as a pair or as a rule that receives the model and the index and returns a pair. Some domains bring bounds of their own:

m.x = pyo.Var(m.S, domain=pyo.Binary)
print(f"x: {len(m.x)} variables, x[P001,2028] in {m.x['P001', 2028].domain}, bounds {m.x['P001', 2028].bounds}")
x: 13 variables, x[P001,2028] in Binary, bounds (0, 1)

One variable per allowed start, and `Binary` implies the bounds 0 and 1. The formulation's $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}\ \forall (i,t) \in S`$ is exactly this line. A variable declared with no domain and no bounds is a free real, unbounded both ways, which is rarely what a model means: say the domain every time, as the formulation does. `pyomo_timing.build(..., integer=False)` swaps `Binary` for `UnitInterval` to get the LP relaxation, the model with every $`x_{i,t}`$ allowed anywhere in $`[0, 1]`$.
A Constraint Rule Writes One Row per Index, and Constraint.Skip Writes None

An indexed `Constraint` takes a **rule**: a function Pyomo calls once per member of the index set, with the model and that member, and which returns one row. A row is a Pyomo relation built with `<=`, `>=` or `==` (or a tuple `(lower, expression, upper)` for a two-sided row). The rule may instead return `pyo.Constraint.Skip`, and then that index gets no row at all:

def once_rule(m, i):
    starts = [m.x[j, t] for j, t in m.S if j == i]
    if len(starts) == 1:
        return pyo.Constraint.Skip       # one start variable: its 0/1 domain already says "at most once"
    return sum(starts) <= 1


m.once = pyo.Constraint(m.P, rule=once_rule)
print("once rows:", [m.once[i].name for i in m.once], f"({len(m.once)} of {len(m.P)} projects)")
print("once[P008]:", m.once["P008"].expr)

Four of the eight tiny projects have a single allowed start, and for them "at most once" is already true of one binary, so the rule skips them (this small example writes only the "at most once" row; `pyomo_timing.py` writes `== 1` for must-do projects, as the formulation says). The row's name is the component's name and its index, `once[P008]`, which is the name a solver log, an infeasibility report or lesson 5.1.4's tools will show you.
Skip is not an optional nicety. A sum over no terms is the Python number 0, so a rule whose sum is empty returns a plain `True` or `False` (here `0 <= 1`), and Pyomo refuses it:

bad: InvalidConstraintError Invalid constraint expression. The constraint expression resolved to a trivial Boolean (True) instead of a Pyomo object. Please modify your rule to return Constraint.Feasible instead of True.

Pyomo also logs the same error, in a few `ERROR:` lines, before raising it; on Run you will see them above this line. The fix is to look at the terms before summing, as `once_rule` does, and return `pyo.Constraint.Skip` when there are none. MathOpt has the same trap: there too an empty sum is the Python number 0, and a row built from it is a `bool` that MathOpt refuses. `pyomo_timing.py`'s budget rule checks for it the same way. A single, unindexed row needs no rule: `pyo.Constraint(expr=...)` takes the relation directly, as the objective takes `pyo.Objective(expr=..., sense=pyo.maximize)`.
HiGHS Solves the Model, and a Scalar Mutable Param Changes Between Solves

A model is solved by a **solver object**. `pyo.SolverFactory("appsi_highs")` makes one for HiGHS, the open-source MILP solver that section 4 used through MathOpt, and its `config` holds the options: `config.mip_gap = 0.0` asks for a proven optimum rather than one within HiGHS's default tolerance (lesson 5.1.2 explains the gap and reads everything a solve returns). `solver.solve(m)` solves the model and loads the answer onto the variables, so `pyo.value(m.x[i])` and `pyo.value(m.total)` read it.

The model here is the smallest selection: GridCap tiny's eight projects $`P`$, each funded at its earliest start or not, with only a budget row. Parameters $`\text{capex}_i`$ and $`\text{value}_i`$ ($k) and one budget $`B`$ ($k); variables $`x_i \in \{0, 1\}`$:

$`B`$ is one number, so its Param has no index set: a **scalar** Param. Declared `mutable=True`, it stays in the row as a name, and assigning to it, `m.budget = b`, sets its value for the next solve. One model, built once, is solved at three budgets:

m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
m.P = pyo.Set(initialize=[p.project_id for p in tiny.projects])
m.capex = pyo.Param(m.P, initialize={p.project_id: p.capex for p in tiny.projects})
m.value = pyo.Param(m.P, initialize={p.project_id: p.value for p in tiny.projects})
m.budget = pyo.Param(initialize=3000, mutable=True)      # no index set: a scalar Param, one number
m.x = pyo.Var(m.P, domain=pyo.Binary)
m.spend = pyo.Constraint(expr=sum(m.capex[i] * m.x[i] for i in m.P) <= m.budget)
m.total = pyo.Objective(expr=sum(m.value[i] * m.x[i] for i in m.P), sense=pyo.maximize)
print("spend row:", m.spend.expr)

solver = pyo.SolverFactory("appsi_highs")       # HiGHS through Pyomo's appsi interface
solver.config.mip_gap = 0.0                     # stop only at a proven optimum
for b in (3000, 5000, 8000):
    m.budget = b                                # assigning to a scalar mutable Param sets its value
    solver.solve(m)
    funded = [i for i in m.P if pyo.value(m.x[i]) > 0.5]
    print(f"budget {pyo.value(m.budget):>5}: value {pyo.value(m.total):>5}, funded {funded}")

The row's right side prints as `budget`, the Param's name, so each solve reads the value assigned just before it, and each budget gets its own plan. An indexed mutable Param is set one entry at a time instead, `m.budget[2027] = 1500`, as the Params section did.

The Port Gives Lesson 6.4.1's Optimum

`pyomo_timing.build` is the whole model of *The Model* above in about forty lines. Two rules worth reading in it: `after_rule` reads the parent and the lag from Params (`m.parent[c]`, `m.lag[c]`), so the rule never touches the portfolio object; and the objective is one `Objective` over `m.S`. The module's programs make their solver with `highs()`, defined at the end of `pyomo_timing.py`: the solver object of the last section, with its gap as an argument.

def highs(gap: float = 0.0):
    """HiGHS through Pyomo's appsi interface, asked for a proven optimum."""
    solver = pyo.SolverFactory("appsi_highs")
    solver.config.mip_gap = gap
    return solver
Solving the port on GridCap small (lesson 5.1.2 is about solving and reading the answer):

import pyomo.environ as pyo

from gridcap import generate
from pyomo_timing import build, highs, schedule

small = generate("small")
m = build(small)
print(f"{len(m.x)} variables, {m.nconstraints()} rows:",
      {c.local_name: len(c) for c in m.component_objects(pyo.Constraint)})
highs().solve(m)
plan = schedule(m)
print(f"NPV ${pyo.value(m.value):,.0f}k")
late = {pid: t for pid, t in plan.items() if t > small.project(pid).earliest_start}
print(f"started {len(plan)} of {len(small.projects)}; {len(late)} later than their earliest year")
by_year = {y: sum(1 for t in plan.values() if t == y) for y in small.years}
print("starts per year:", by_year)

Every line matches lesson 6.4.1's MathOpt output, shown at the top of this lesson: $24,260k, 27 projects started, 9 deferred, and the same starts per year. The module's tests go further and check, on tiny and small, as MILP and as LP relaxation, that the two models have the same number of variables and rows and the same optimum, and that they choose the same start year for every project. Two independent builds of one formulation agreeing is the cheapest proof that neither has a typo in a row, the check lesson 6.6.4 made between MathOpt and Pyomo's `Piecewise`.

`m.component_objects(pyo.Constraint)` walks the model's constraint components (`once`, `alt`, ...); `m.component_data_objects(pyo.Var)` walks every single variable. These two calls are how you inspect any Pyomo model you are handed.
Summary

items: **A ConcreteModel is built from data you already have.** Components are attached as attributes, and the attribute name is the component's name.
**Sets name the indices, and a set of pairs keeps a sparse index sparse.** `m.S` holds the 13 allowed starts on tiny where the cross product has 24.
**Params hold the data, and a mutable Param can change after the build.** `default=` fills indices inside the set; an index outside it is an error; a mutable Param stays a name in its rows.
**A Var takes its domain and bounds from its declaration.** `Binary` brings bounds (0, 1).
**A Constraint rule writes one row per index, and Constraint.Skip writes none.** A rule that returns `True` or `False` is refused.
**HiGHS solves the model, and a scalar mutable Param changes between solves.** `SolverFactory("appsi_highs")` with `config.mip_gap = 0.0`; `m.budget = b` sets a scalar Param.
**The port gives lesson 6.4.1's optimum.** $24,260k with the same plan, checked by the tests.

[MO-book](https://mobook.github.io/MO-book/), *Hands-On Mathematical Optimization with Python*, whose notebooks build every model in Pyomo in the style of this lesson.
Challenges

items: Build `m.S` as the cross product `m.P * m.Y` instead, and give the out-of-window starts a fixed value of 0 (`m.x[i, t].fix(0)`). Count the variables Pyomo hands to the solver, and compare.
Change `m.budget` on the small model to 4,000 in 2030 and 2031 and re-solve without rebuilding. Lesson 5.1.4 explains what comes back.
Write the alternative-group row with `m.members[g]` but without the helper `started`.

blocks.text: Design Note: One Formulation, Two Builds, One Test

Porting a model is a translation, and translations have typos. The module's tests build the MathOpt model of lesson 6.4.1 and the Pyomo model of this lesson from the same portfolio and compare the optimum, the sizes and the plan. Keep such a test whenever two implementations of one model live side by side: the day one of them changes alone, the test says so.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**first_model.py.** Builds a model on GridCap tiny one component at a time and prints what Pyomo made of each (*Sets*, *Params*, *A Var*, *A Constraint Rule*). *Try:* Give `m.npv` a `default=0` and ask for `npv["P001", 2027]` again. Predict whether the error changes.

**first_solve.py.** The one-budget selection on GridCap tiny, solved with HiGHS at three budgets by assigning the scalar mutable Param (*HiGHS Solves the Model*). *Try:* Add 2,000 to the list of budgets. Predict which projects it funds before you run it.
**port_check.py.** Solves the ported model on GridCap small (*The Port Gives Lesson 6.4.1's Optimum*). *Try:* Build it with `integer=False` and print the LP relaxation's NPV.
**pyomo_timing.py.** The Pyomo model builder, with `schedule` to read the plan and `highs` to make a solver. It runs nothing itself.
